title: Striped garter baby blanket
subtitle: A two-colour garter blanket with four-row stripes, for a cot.
excerpt: A 75 by 90 cm cot blanket worked flat in garter stitch with four-row stripes alternating between two DK colours. The yarn is carried up the side edge to avoid cutting and rejoining at every stripe. About 130 g of each colour.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 4th series (1888), §Striped Baby Wraps, describes stripe sequences worked in garter stitch as a standard beginner nursery project. The technique of carrying yarn up the side edge to avoid cutting appears in the same source.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked.

stitchCountCheckpoints.label: Halfway check — 165 sts, about 24 stripes completed

glossaryTerms.definition: Instead of cutting the unused yarn at every stripe change, twisting the working yarn loosely around the waiting strand every two rows to keep it anchored against the edge. The carried yarn runs up the side of the blanket and the ends to weave in are reduced to two per colour.

content.text: A single-panel rectangle worked flat in garter stitch with four-row stripes in two DK colours, finishing at 75 cm wide by 90 cm long.

Single-panel construction gives a blanket with no seams to open in the wash. Four-row stripes were chosen over two-row stripes because each colour always changes at the same edge of the blanket, making it possible to
carry both yarns up the side edge

without cutting and rejoining. This cuts the number of ends from nearly 100 (one for each stripe) to four total. Budget about 130 g of each colour (about 285 m / 310 yards per colour) of machine-washable DK. Buy both colours at once in matched dye lots within each colour; mismatched lots of the same nominal colour show a horizontal line at the change. Drapes across a cot or folds flat for a pram bag.
What you need

items.name: Yarn A (main colour)
items.qty: 130 g (about 285 m / 310 yards) of DK-weight machine-washable yarn
items.substitutions: Superwash merino DK. Choose a colour with good contrast against Colour B so the stripes read clearly.

items.name: Yarn B (contrast colour)
items.qty: 130 g (about 285 m / 310 yards) of the same DK yarn in a contrasting or complementary colour

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) straight or circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked. The stripe colour changes do not affect gauge. Work a swatch in one colour at least 15 cm square, leave it flat overnight, and measure the centre 10 cm.

If your row gauge is 40 rows per 10 cm instead of 44, the blanket will be about 10 cm shorter at the same total row count (396 rows gives about 99 cm rather than 90 cm). A four-row stripe at 40 rows per 10 cm is about 2.5 mm shorter per stripe: over 99 stripes this accumulates to roughly 25 mm total length loss. Measure the length by tape rather than by counting stripes.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on
Using Yarn A and the long-tail cast-on, cast on 165 stitches. Long-tail tail: (4 × 165) / 10 + 15 = 81 cm. Measure 90 cm of tail before starting; round up to 110 cm to be safe.
Stripe sequence
Rows 1 to 4: using Yarn A, knit all 4 rows.

Rows 5 to 8: drop Yarn A at the left-hand edge. Pick up Yarn B, leaving a 10 cm tail if this is the first time. Knit 4 rows with Yarn B. At the start of rows 5 and 7, twist Yarn A loosely around Yarn B at the left edge to anchor it.

Repeat this 8-row sequence (4 rows Yarn A, 4 rows Yarn B) until the blanket measures 90 cm from the cast-on. Always change colour at the same edge. The finished blanket will have approximately 99 stripes of 4 rows each.
When you set this aside, jot the current row within the stripe and which yarn you are on. Picking up mid-stripe is easy once you know where you are in the repeat.
Stitch count check-ins
After 24 complete stripes (96 rows, about 22 cm): count across the needle. You should have 165 stitches.
Before the final cast-off row (about row 392, 89 cm): count again. You should still have 165 stitches.
Common faults

Carried yarn too tight along the side edge: the blanket puckers on the left side where Yarn A was twisted too firmly against Yarn B. Carry the unused yarn loosely; it only needs to be held against the edge, not pulled taut.

Yarn colour changing on the wrong edge: both yarns end up on the same side of the blanket. This happens if the colour was switched partway through a stripe rather than at the full four-row count. Keep a tally of rows within each stripe if this is a risk.

Ladder at the colour-change column: the first stitch of each new stripe is worked slightly loose, leaving a visible vertical line of looser stitches on one edge. Snug the first stitch of each colour a little tighter than the rest; this usually resolves after blocking.
Cast-off
Using whichever yarn is at the needle when you reach 90 cm, cast off all stitches knitwise with a relaxed tension.
Finishing

Weave in the four yarn tails (start and end of each colour) on the wrong side along garter ridges for at least 5 cm each, changing direction once. The carried-yarn side edge does not need further attention once the tails are woven. Trim.
Care
Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble dry. Colours in superwash merino remain stable through repeated washes when the initial skeins were in matched lots.
What to try next

Once the stripe carry technique is comfortable, try a three-colour stripe rotation: each colour shifts one position every four rows. The carry is the same but you twist three strands at the edge, which keeps the fabric neater than cutting and rejoining. After that, a simple Fair Isle baby blanket uses the same DK yarn and needle size but works two strands at once across each row.
